sources.summary: Apple’s tone-deaf Karate Kid knock-off feels like a Maga-approved after-school special It’s hard to avoid the reports that boys and young men are in trouble . Across the US and UK, they’re outpaced by girls on reading tests, are more likely to have behavioral difficulties and exposed to impossible body image standards by the manosphere. You might think that all of this would make you think extra carefully about a film that centers on a 13-year-old boy. Not in the case of Way of the Warrior Kid, a cliche-ridden celebration of machismo and the military that greets the current climate with a shrug. At times, I had to remind myself that I wasn’t watching a Maga-funded after-school special. Continue reading...

sources.summary: The Great White Hope, All the President’s Men, Kramer vs Kramer … Alexander has a CV most actors can only dream of. She talks us through the highs and lows – including a ‘beautiful’ encounter with Muhammad Ali Jane Alexander will never forget the play that won her a Tony award, a husband and her first film role. The Great White Hope, which ran on Broadway from 1968 to 1970, was based on the life of Black boxer Jack Johnson, who in 1908 became world heavyweight champion in segregated America. Alexander played Eleanor, a white woman married to an African American boxer also called Jack, at a time when interracial marriages were still illegal in many states. Decades later, when the play opened, the US supreme court had only recently struck down all remaining bans – and Alexander received hate mail and death threats for the role. Continue reading...

sources.summary: Rob a bank to the sound of Sibelius, mow down an alligator to the music of Mahler … piano sensation Yuja Wang is one of the surprises of GTA VI – and her thrilling musical choices made me crash into a G-Wagen I blame Yuja Wang for crashing my car. You know how it is, you’re cruising as fast you can on the freeway, listening to Symphony FM. And then DJ Yuja says: “It’s afternoon here in Vice City: for the worst of you, the day is just starting. Maybe the next piece will inspire you to turn your life around.” And then she played Tchaikovsky – the finale of the Fifth Symphony – and I just lost it to the music. The energy and tempest of the finale turned me into a driving maniac, and I ended up crashing into a G-Wagen down a one-way street as the minor-key maelstrom took over. Thanks Yuja. I’ll send you the repair bill. Such are the hazards of discovering that among the 24 stations you can listen to in Grand Theft Auto VI – and not only in your car – is Symphony FM, hosted by the in-game Yuja, who really is the real-life piano superstar Yuja Wang . And in choosing her “favourite pieces and curating a playlist for players to discover”, she’s put together a set of 16 pieces that only she could have come up with. Continue reading...

sources.summary: (Atlantic) Justice bring some 80s nostalgia but this compilation of new material from music’s A-list – from Dua Lipa to Travis Scott and a host of Latin talent – stays at the cutting edge It can be hard to ascertain why Grand Theft Auto VI is such a phenomenon from merely watching along with it. Equally devoted to the thrill of a violent crime story and a more mundane lifestyle fantasy, the appeal does not always translate to bystanders. Its soundtrack, however, is another story: a compilation of brand new material from some of the biggest pop, rap, rock and country artists on the planet – some of them combined in imaginative pileups of guest features – that can be enjoyed totally separately from the gameplay, if you so wish. Starting from Zero, the opener by Justice – also composers of the game’s original score, released on 11 December – features the unmistakable voice of the Doobie Brothers’ Michael McDonald belting out an 80s-style pop ballad complete with a saxophone outro. This style is synonymous with Grand Theft Auto VI’s setting, a fictionalised version of Florida last seen in 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City, which was beloved for its inclusion of 80s hits. sources.summary: Read Darkroom by Meher Iqbal – this year’s winner of the Guardian and publisher 4th Estate’s award for unpublished writers of colour Meher Iqbal wins 2026 4thWrite prize with ‘evocative’ coming-of-age story • Content warning: This story includes a description of a sexual assault Nadia and I lay on the asphalt road, playing our favourite game for the last time. My older brother Abdullah had taught it to me when I was nine: lie down on a speed bump, legs long and both arms outstretched by your ears, making your body a long pencil. I was in the wrong position that day – it was so hot that the backs of my shins seared when they touched the road, so I had to bend my knees. Nadia wasn’t allowed to have her legs exposed anymore, so her linen trousers protected her. The game was intuitive – when you hear a car coming, roll down the slope and run away as fast you can. If you turned around only to find that the car was a decent way away, you were a baby. Abdullah never explained the underlying objective to me, but I think he enjoyed how much it agitated and scared adults at the same time. Simple and stupid, like most things he taught me at that age, but I liked that it gave me an opportunity to see just how fast I could run; the 100-metre track at school never drew out of me what running for my life did. Nadia didn’t care about any of that, but she humoured me anyway. Continue reading...
